clue.text: Argentinian hero left with King George to gatecrash party

indicators.note: to gatecrash is to push one's way into a party, so these letters are pushed inside the party word

parts.note: a beano is an informal British word for a party or celebration
GR stands for Georgius Rex, King George, as on British postboxes

explanation.surface: A national hero of Argentina turns up uninvited at a party with a British monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' could be any celebration; here it is the British slang word for a knees-up, which takes in left and the royal cipher of King George.
explanation.definitionFit: Manuel Belgrano was a leader of Argentina's independence struggle and designed its flag.

clue.text: Debts repudiated by scholarly boss

indicators.note: the debts are disowned, thrown out of the scholarly word they sit in

parts.note: studious means given to study, scholarly
IOUs are written promises to pay, debts

explanation.surface: A learned employer refuses to honour what is owed.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove IOUS from STUDIOUS, leaving the front four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is a raised ornamental knob, the same as a stud on a shield or door.

clue.text: Blunt, it may be said, is sound

indicators.note: it may be said signals that the word for blunt is spoken, and a same-sounding word is entered

parts.note: blunt, plain-speaking, means straight

explanation.surface: A remark that frank talk is wholesome.
explanation.definitionFit: A sound is a narrow channel of sea between two landmasses, a geographical synonym.

clue.text: Casually read about Bryson's conclusion on a small island

indicators.note: about here means around, so the reading word goes round the final letter

parts.note: to browse is to read casually

indicators.note: the conclusion of Bryson's is its last letter

explanation.surface: Skimming a Bill Bryson travel book's final chapter about a little British island.
explanation.walkthrough: BROWSE wraps N (the end of Bryson) to give BROWNSE, then A follows. Brownsea Island lies in Poole Harbour, Dorset, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Brownsea is a small island in Poole Harbour, birthplace of the Scout movement.

clue.text: Down-to-earth approach with soldiers in fight

indicators.note: in places the soldiers inside the phrase for the descent

parts.note: free fall is a parachutist's plunge toward the ground before the chute opens
OR, other ranks, means ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: Soldiers parachuting into a battle zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down-to-earth' looks like 'practical', but it is literal: a skydiver's fall to the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A free-for-all is a chaotic brawl in which everyone joins, a fight.

clue.text: Pawn toast

definitions.meaning: to pawn is to hand over something as security
to toast someone is to drink their health

explanation.definitionFit: Pledge means both give as security and drink a health to someone, two dictionary senses.

clue.text: Dry old Tory leader Attlee turned round

indicators.note: turned round asks for the letters to be spun about into a new order
the leader of Tory is its first letter

parts.note: taken as written; Clement Attlee was a Labour prime minister

explanation.surface: A former Conservative chief and Labour PM Attlee spun into a sober politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Attlee was a British Labour prime minister, so a Tory leader beside him jars. O, T and ATTLEE are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Dry describes someone who abstains from alcohol, as does teetotal.

clue.text: Folks ignored Larkin poem about US city

indicators.note: ignored means the relatives' word is left out of the poet's name

parts.note: one's folks are one's kin, relatives

indicators.note: about here means turned around, so the poem word runs backwards

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: Relatives disregarded a poem by Philip Larkin about an American town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Larkin poem' suggests a title, but Larkin just loses KIN to give LAR; ODE backwards is EDO.
explanation.definitionFit: Laredo is a city in Texas on the Mexican border.

clue.text: Hardly ever very well

definitions.meaning: an old sense meaning exceptionally or splendidly well

explanation.definitionFit: Rarely means seldom, and in an older usage it meant finely or excellently.

clue.text: Old silver mine found at last

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

indicators.note: at last picks the final letter of each of the two words

explanation.surface: An ancient silver mine finally discovered.
explanation.definitionFit: Aged means elderly or of great age, a simple synonym.

clue.text: Schoolmasters not initially providing archery tips?

indicators.note: not initially means the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: Harrow is a famous English public school
heads are head teachers, masters in charge of schools

explanation.surface: Teachers failing to give pupils pointers on shooting bows.
explanation.walkthrough: Harrow is a leading English private school, so its heads are schoolmasters; drop the H.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrowheads are the pointed tips of arrows used in archery.

clue.text: Baskerville's lead plus hound

indicators.note: a lead is what goes in front, so the first letter of the name

parts.note: a plus is an advantage, an asset

explanation.surface: The Baskervilles' famous dog on its leash, an evocation of Conan Doyle's hound.
explanation.definitionFit: A basset is a short-legged breed of hunting dog.

clue.text: Composer from Southampton, when concealing English name

parts.note: Southampton FC, the English football club, is nicknamed the Saints

indicators.note: concealing means the time word hides the two letters inside it

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as he left'

explanation.surface: A musician from the south-coast port keeps his English name under wraps.
explanation.walkthrough: Southampton is an English port city whose football club are the Saints; AS hides EN.
explanation.definitionFit: Camille Saint-Saens was a French composer, of The Carnival of the Animals.

clue.text: Dire bod's shockingly laid bare

indicators.note: shockingly suggests the letters are scandalously jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; the apostrophe adds no letter

explanation.surface: An awful bloke's body exposed, scandalously.
explanation.definitionFit: Disrobed means undressed, stripped of clothing, so exposed.

clue.text: City in the Peloponnese, in the Adriatic or in Thessaly

indicators.note: in here means contained within the run of letters that follows

explanation.surface: A quiz question placing a Greek city amid regions of Greece and its seas.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters lie across Adriatic, or, in and Thessaly.
explanation.definitionFit: Corinth is an ancient Greek city on the isthmus joining the Peloponnese to the mainland.

clue.text: Hitchcock's work? Be upset in parts

indicators.note: in means the overturned word goes inside the parts word

parts.note: thirds are parts of a whole

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so read backwards

explanation.surface: A film-buff remark about getting upset during scenes of a Hitchcock movie.
explanation.definitionFit: The Birds is a 1963 Alfred Hitchcock thriller, one of his films.

clue.text: People in Asia expressed discomfort

indicators.note: expressed means spoken, so the word is matched by its sound

parts.note: the Malays are a people of Malaysia and nearby Southeast Asia

explanation.surface: Asian people voicing their unease.
explanation.definitionFit: Malaise is a general feeling of unease or illness, a discomfort.

clue.text: People brought in without armoured personnel carriers

indicators.note: brought in means placed inside the word for without

parts.note: sans means without
a race is a people

explanation.surface: Folk admitted with no military vehicles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'People' looks like the definition, as Saracens were a people, but it is RACE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Saracen was a British six-wheeled armoured vehicle used to carry troops.

clue.text: Rockers, for example, providing church music

parts.note: airs are tunes, music

explanation.surface: Rock musicians supplying hymns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rockers' suggests musicians, but means rocking chairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A rocker is a rocking chair, so rockers are an example of seats.

clue.text: Ruby has lace inside out

indicators.note: inside means the lace word sits within the other word

parts.note: forth means out, as in 'go forth'
to lace is to tie

explanation.surface: A girl called Ruby wears her lace inside out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruby' seems a name, but a ruby wedding marks forty years of marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruby anniversary celebrates the fortieth year of a marriage.

clue.text: Herb, not the first to have mounted wild ass

indicators.note: mounted in a down clue means climbing upward, so the letters read backwards
not the first means the opening letter is removed

parts.note: oregano is a culinary herb

explanation.surface: A man named Herb, lacking first place, rides a wild donkey.
explanation.walkthrough: Oregano loses its first O to give REGANO, which 'mounted' turns upward.
explanation.definitionFit: An onager is a wild ass of Asia, a type of equine.

clue.text: Poussins, say, given area — not where French like chicken feed

indicators.note: not, with given, means the area letter is put in place of the French word

parts.note: poussins are young chickens, an example of poultry
the French for where is ou

explanation.surface: Young chickens on a patch of ground, with no French bird food.
explanation.walkthrough: POULTRY swaps OU (French 'where') for A. 'Chicken feed' looks literal but means a trifling sum.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicken feed is slang for a trivial amount, so meagre or trifling.

clue.text: Cannon and Ball for decoration?

definitions.meaning: a woolly ball used to trim a hat

explanation.definitionFit: A pom-pom is a light automatic gun and also a decorative woolly ball, two separate senses.

clue.text: Maniacs fit to bust — displaying this

definitions.text: Maniacs fit to bust — displaying this

indicators.note: to bust is to break apart, so the letters burst into new order

explanation.surface: Madmen ready to explode show the wild zeal named.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanaticism is excessive, frenzied zeal, the trait shown by people frantic to the point of bursting.

clue.text: Hammer film with decapitation

indicators.note: decapitation removes the head, the first letter

parts.note: a flick is a film

explanation.surface: A Hammer horror movie featuring a beheading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hammer' suggests Hammer Films, the British horror studio, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To lick an opponent is to beat or thrash them soundly, informally.

clue.text: Storage area full of tuck boxes

indicators.note: boxes means holds within, so the letters sit inside the phrase

explanation.surface: A school storeroom crammed with tuck boxes.
explanation.walkthrough: Tuck is British school slang for sweets and snacks; a tuck box holds them.
explanation.definitionFit: A loft is a space under the roof used for storing things.

clue.text: Housing in which eastern sailors drink

indicators.note: in which means the following letters are placed within the housing word

parts.note: a pod is a casing or housing, as for an engine
RN, the Royal Navy, supplies sailors

explanation.surface: A building where sailors from the East have a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Pernod is a French aniseed-flavoured aperitif, a brand of drink.

clue.text: Derisively speaking with one's mouth full?

explanation.definitionFit: Scoffing means mocking and, in British slang, wolfing down food: two senses.
